Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$ C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}. $$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$ X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1, $$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$ \Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}). $$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$ N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}. $$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$ \ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right]. $$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$ \widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases} $$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$ \sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2. $$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Uniformly for $\alpha\le A$, for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $\log N_\alpha\ge8$, $\lceil N_\alpha/\rho\rceil\ge N_0$, $\log N_\alpha\ge2\log\rho$ and $(1+\rho/N_\alpha)^{r_\alpha}\le2$.
Temporarily suppress $\alpha$ from $r,s,N,V$.
For a polished-tail truth put $m=\lceil N/\rho\rceil$, $B=\{m,\ldots,\lfloor\rho m\rfloor\}$ and $E_B=\sum_{i\in B}\theta_i^2$.
For every $i$, $f_\alpha(i)\le2N^s\log N$.

Differentiation under the signal sum is valid by domination by a bounded multiplier of $\theta_i^2$, since its tail and each of its first derivatives are bounded by a constant times $i^{-1-4p}(\log i)^k$.
Set $t_i=i^{1+2\alpha}\kappa_i^{-2}$ and $a_i=n^2t_i\log i/(t_i+n)^2$.

For $j=0,1$ the preceding identities give
$$ \operatorname{Var}_\theta Q_n^{(j)}(\alpha)\le K N_\alpha(\log N_\alpha)^{2+2j}(1+h_\alpha).
The random sums have common versions suitable for integration and suprema.
Put $R_\alpha=Q_n(\alpha)/G_\alpha$.
Write $\lambda=\log(\rho\vee e)\ge1$ and $t=\sqrt{\log n}$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$ \log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x). $$

$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

$$ \inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1. $$

In the defined inverse Gaussian procedure write $q=1+2\alpha+2p$, $N=N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/q}$, $R=N^{-2\alpha}=N^{1+2p}/n$, $B_i(\alpha)=-i^{1+2\alpha}\theta_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$, and $W_i(\alpha)=\sqrt n\kappa_i Z_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$. derivations.claim: Write $a=a_n$, $b=b_n$.
On the bracket event from [F2], the case $\widehat\alpha_n=0$ gives coverage by [F1].
For fixed $A$, [F2] bounds $R_a/R_b$ by a constant depending only on the fixed parameters.
For growing $A_n$, the sharpened comparison in [F2] bounds $R_a/R_b$ by $K(1+L_0\rho^{1+2A_n})^{1+2p}$.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, and $0<\alpha<\infty$ in the
procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]]. Put
$r=1+2\alpha$. Then the product prior is supported on $\ell^2$, and its
posterior kernel under the prior-predictive law $Q_{n,\alpha}$ is the product
of the coordinate laws
$$ N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1, $$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is
supported on $\ell^2$, and its posterior mean belongs to $\ell^2$.

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and
$$ \log\frac{dQ_{n,\alpha}}{dQ_{n,0}}(x) =-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^r}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right] =\ell_n(\alpha;x). $$
The density identity and absolute convergence hold $Q_{n,0}$-almost surely.
The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

Use the inverse Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and $\kappa_i^2\in[C^{-2}i^{-2p},C^2i^{-2p}]$.
Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. Let
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ with $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A]$, put
$$ N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/(1+2\alpha+2p)},\qquad h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)= \frac{1+2\alpha+2p}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2 i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_{0,i}^2} {(i^{1+2\alpha+2p}+n)^2}. $$
Define
$$ \underline\alpha_n= \inf\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\ge(16C^8)^{-1}\}, \qquad \overline\alpha_n= \sup\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\le8C^8\}, $$
with the source conventions $\inf\varnothing=A$ and $\sup\varnothing=0$.
Then the source bracket result is
$$ \inf_{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho),\,\theta_{0,1}=0} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)} \bigl(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n\bigr) \longrightarrow1. $$
More generally, the same conclusion holds with $A=A_n$ whenever
$$ 0<A_n\le\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}} $$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Uniformly in the polished-tail class, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$ \frac{n^{-2\underline\alpha_n/(1+2\underline\alpha_n+2p)}}{n^{-2\overline\alpha_n/(1+2\overline\alpha_n+2p)}}\le\left[128C^{16}\{4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A_n}\}\right]^{1+2p}. $$
In particular, for fixed $A$ the two rates are uniformly comparable. The lower bracket alone is valid uniformly over arbitrary $\theta_0\in\ell^2$, using the same definition of $\underline\alpha_n$ and the same procedure/domain hypotheses:
$$ \inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1. $$

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The recursion gives $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$.
Put $\delta_j=s\log\rho_j/(4\log n_j)$, $a_j=\beta+\delta_j$, $t_j=s+2\delta_j$ and $d=1+2p$.
For $x\ge2$ and $q\ge2$, split the integers $i>x$ into intervals $(2^l x,2^{l+1}x]$.
Set $n=n_j$ and first take $0\le\alpha\le\beta$.
Now take $\beta<\alpha\le a_j$, and write $\delta=\alpha-\beta$, $t=s+2\delta$, $K=n^{1/t}$, $N=N_j$ and $\rho=\rho_j$.
For the middle part use $(i^t+n)^2\ge i^{2t}$, $\log i\le\log(2N)$ and at most $2N$ indices, obtaining $H_2\le2M(\log(2N)/\log K)n^2N^{1-2s-2\delta}/K$.
For the last part set $q=2s+2\delta\ge2$ and apply step 2.1 at $x=\rho N$.

For fixed $\alpha$ write $B_i(\alpha)=i^{1+2\alpha}\theta_{0,i}/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$ and $W_i(\alpha)=\sqrt n\kappa_i Z_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$, so the posterior-mean error is $-B(\alpha)+W(\alpha)$.
For every realization of the normal coordinates, $|W_i(\alpha)|\le|W_i(a_j)|$ whenever $\alpha\ge a_j$.
Subtracting exponents and using $n_j^{\delta_j}=\rho_j^{s/4}$ gives $R_j/N_j^{-\beta}=\rho_j^{-d/(4t_j)}$.
On $E_j$ the selected regularity is positive and at least $a_j$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$ \sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2. $$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$ \inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1. $$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a growing
$A=A_n$ provided
$$ A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}. $$
In that case a slowly varying inflation sequence is required; the source
allows $L_n\lesssim(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$.

derivations.claim: The sequence is square summable because $\sum_{i=2}^\infty i^{-1-2\beta}\le 1+\int_1^\infty x^{-1-2\beta}\,dx<\infty$.

For $N\ge2$, monotonicity of $x^{-1-2\beta}$ gives $\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}i^{-1-2\beta} \le N^{-1-2\beta}+\int_N^\infty x^{-1-2\beta}\,dx \le \left(1+\frac1{2\beta}\right)N^{-2\beta}$ and $\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}i^{-1-2\beta} \ge\int_N^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor+1}x^{-1-2\beta}\,dx \ge\frac{1-\rho^{-2\beta}}{2\beta}N^{-2\beta}.$ Multiplying by $M$ shows that the tail-to-block ratio is at most $(2\beta+1)/(1-\rho^{-2\beta})=L_0$, so [F2] holds.
The truth has $\theta_{0,1}=0$ and satisfies [F2], so the theorem [F3] supplies a sufficiently large inflation for which its frequentist coverage tends to one.

citations.quote:
Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$ \Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}. $$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

1.1 The recursion gives $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$. The preceding last gap endpoint satisfies $\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}\le N_j/(2\rho_j)<N_j$, while the next first gap begins at $N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}N_j>2N_j$. Thus no other zero gap intersects $N_j<i\le2N_j$, where $\theta_{0,i}^2=Mi^{-1-2\beta}$. Every squared coordinate is zero or $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$, so $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M(1+(2\beta)^{-1})<\infty$ and [F3] holds. Finally $1<N_1=2^{1/s}<2=\rho_1$, so the first gap contains coordinate $1$. [F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Put $\delta_j=s\log\rho_j/(4\log n_j)$, $a_j=\beta+\delta_j$, $t_j=s+2\delta_j$ and $d=1+2p$. Iterating the growth bound gives $\log n_j\ge\log2+s(\log2)(j^2+2j-3)$ for $j\ge2$, hence $\delta_j\to0$. Consequently, eventually $0<\delta_j\le1/4$, $a_j<A$, $N_j/\rho_j\ge2$ and $N_j\ge2$. Restrict to these indices and put $T=s+1/2$, so $s<t_j\le T$ and $n_j^{\delta_j}=\rho_j^{s/4}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 For $x\ge2$ and $q\ge2$, split the integers $i>x$ into intervals $(2^l x,2^{l+1}x]$. Each contains at most $3\cdot2^l x$ integers, and $\log i\le(l+2)\log x$. Hence $\sum_{i>x}i^{-q}\log i\le3x^{1-q}\log x\sum_{l\ge0}(l+2)2^{-l(q-1)}\le18x^{1-q}\log x$, because $\sum_{l\ge0}(l+2)2^{-l}=6$. [algebra]

2.2 Set $n=n_j$ and first take $0\le\alpha\le\beta$. Write $t=1+2\alpha+2p$, $K=n^{1/t}$ and $q=2+2\alpha+4p+2\beta\ge2$. In [F2], use the denominator bounds $(i^t+n)^2\ge n^2$ for $i\le K$ and $(i^t+n)^2\ge i^{2t}$ for $i>K$, together with $\theta_{0,i}^2\le Mi^{-1-2\beta}$. The first part of $h_n(\alpha)$ is at most $M$, since $i^{2\alpha-2\beta}\le1$ and $\sum_{i\le K}\log i\le K\log K$. By step 2.1 the tail is at most $18Mn^2K^{-q}=18MK^{2\alpha-2\beta}\le18M$. Thus $h_n(\alpha)\le19M$ throughout $[0,\beta]$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

2.3 Now take $\beta<\alpha\le a_j$, and write $\delta=\alpha-\beta$, $t=s+2\delta$, $K=n^{1/t}$, $N=N_j$ and $\rho=\rho_j$. The zero gaps split $h_n$ into three nonnegative parts, over $i\le N/\rho$, $N<i\le2N$ and $i>\rho N$. Bounding the denominator by $n^2$, the first part satisfies $H_1\le M(\log N/\log K)(N/\rho)^{1+2\delta}/K$. Here $\log N/\log K=t/s\le T/s$ and $N^{1+2\delta}/K=n^{2\delta(t+1)/(st)}\le\rho^{(s+1)/(2s)}$, using $\delta\le\delta_j$ and $(t+1)/t\le(s+1)/s$. Therefore $H_1\le M(T/s)\rho^{-(s-1)/(2s)}$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.4 For the middle part use $(i^t+n)^2\ge i^{2t}$, $\log i\le\log(2N)$ and at most $2N$ indices, obtaining $H_2\le2M(\log(2N)/\log K)n^2N^{1-2s-2\delta}/K$. Since $N\ge2$, the logarithm ratio is at most $2T/s$. Also $n^2N^{1-2s-2\delta}/K=n^{-2\delta(t-1)/(st)}\le1$. Consequently $H_2\le4MT/s$. [step 1.2, step 2.3, algebra]

2.5 For the last part set $q=2s+2\delta\ge2$ and apply step 2.1 at $x=\rho N$. This gives $H_3\le18M(\log(\rho N)/\log K)n^2(\rho N)^{1-q}/K$. Because $\log\rho/\log N=4\delta_j\le1$, the logarithm ratio is at most $2T/s$. Furthermore $n^2N^{1-q}/K=n^{-2\delta(t-1)/(st)}\le1$ and $\rho^{1-q}\le\rho^{1-2s}$. Thus $H_3\le36M(T/s)\rho^{1-2s}$. Combining these estimates yields $\sup_{0\le\alpha\le a_j}h_n(\alpha)\le\max(19,41T/s)M\le62M\le(32C^8)^{-1}<\tau$, since $s>1$. Hence $\underline\alpha_{n_j}\ge a_j$, and [F2] gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}(E_j)\to1$ for $E_j=\{\widehat\alpha_{n_j}\ge a_j\}$. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, algebra]

3.1 For fixed $\alpha$ write $B_i(\alpha)=i^{1+2\alpha}\theta_{0,i}/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$ and $W_i(\alpha)=\sqrt n\kappa_i Z_i/(i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2)$, so the posterior-mean error is $-B(\alpha)+W(\alpha)$. If $\alpha\ge a_j>\beta$ and $N_j<i\le2N_j$, then $i^{1+2\alpha+2p}\ge N_j^s=n$ and $n\kappa_i^2/i^{1+2\alpha}\le C^2$. There are at least $N_j/2$ integers in this block, each with squared truth at least $M(2N_j)^{-1-2\beta}$. Therefore, uniformly for $\alpha\ge a_j$, $\|B(\alpha)\|^2\ge b^2MN_j^{-2\beta}$, where $b=2^{-1-\beta}/(1+C^2)>0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.2 Set $R_j=n_j^{-a_j/t_j}$ and $D=C^2(2+2^{2\beta+1/2}/(2\beta))$. At $\alpha=a_j$, put $K=n_j^{1/t_j}\ge2$. Since $v_i(a_j)\le C^2i^{2p}/(i^{t_j}+n_j)$, summing over $i\le K$ gives at most $2C^2K^{-2a_j}$. The tail is at most $\sum_{i>K}i^{-1-2a_j}\le\lfloor K\rfloor^{-2a_j}/(2a_j)\le2^{2\beta+1/2}K^{-2a_j}/(2\beta)$. Thus $V_j=\sum_i v_i(a_j)\le DR_j^2$. Each variance decreases in $\alpha$, so [F4] bounds the posterior expected squared centered norm by $V_j$ whenever $\alpha\ge a_j$. For a nonnegative random variable $Y$, integrating $u\mathbf1_{\{Y>u\}}\le Y$ gives $uP(Y>u)\le EY$. Apply this with $u=V_j/\gamma$ to bound the posterior norm quantile: $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\alpha)\le\sqrt{D/\gamma}\,R_j$. [F1, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.3 For every realization of the normal coordinates, $|W_i(\alpha)|\le|W_i(a_j)|$ whenever $\alpha\ge a_j$. Hence $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}\|W(\alpha)\|\le\|W(a_j)\|$. By [F4], $E\|W(a_j)\|^2=\sum_i n_j\kappa_i^2/(i^{1+2a_j}+n_j\kappa_i^2)^2\le V_j\le DR_j^2$. The elementary probability bound proved in step 3.2 therefore gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}\|W(\alpha)\|>b\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta}/2\}\le4DR_j^2/(b^2MN_j^{-2\beta})$. These bounds also show almost sure square-summability simultaneously for every $\alpha\ge a_j$. [F4, step 3.2, algebra]

4.1 Subtracting exponents and using $n_j^{\delta_j}=\rho_j^{s/4}$ gives $R_j/N_j^{-\beta}=\rho_j^{-d/(4t_j)}$. Put $e=d/(4(s+1))$ and $\eta=d/(8(s+1)(s+1/2))>0$. Since $t_j\le T=s+1/2$, one has $d/(4t_j)-e\ge\eta$. The inflation assumption and step 3.2 imply $\sup_{\alpha\ge a_j}L_{n_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\alpha)/(\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta})\le K_L\sqrt{D/\gamma}\,\rho_j^{-\eta}\to0$. Step 3.3's probability bound is at most $(4D/(b^2M))\rho_j^{-d/(2T)}\to0$. [given, step 1.2, step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra]

4.2 On $E_j$ the selected regularity is positive and at least $a_j$. Coverage then implies $\|B(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})\|\le L_{n_j}r_{n_j,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})+\|W(\widehat\alpha_{n_j})\|$. The left side is at least $b\sqrt M N_j^{-\beta}$ by step 3.1; the first term on the right is eventually strictly below half that amount by step 4.1, while the second exceeds the same half-threshold with probability tending to zero. Consequently coverage is at most $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}(E_j^c)+o(1)\to0$. This fixed truth in $\Theta_\beta(M)$ refutes the proposed uniform nonvanishing coverage. [step 2.5, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

derivations.claim: The growth condition implies $N_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}^2N_j$, so $N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}\ge2\rho_{j+1}N_j\ge2\rho_jN_j$.
The construction and its cap, credibility level and small-$M$ assumptions match [F2].
